title: Versola — Database
description: The database as each service sees it: connection pool, query latency, write-ahead log, table sizes and expired-row cleanup. Pick the service at the top. Host metrics (CPU, disk, replication) come from the database platform, not from here.

panels.title: DB pool
panels.description: Share of database connections checked out. Near 100% requests start queueing for a connection. Empty if `postgres.pool-metrics-interval` is not set for this service.

panels.title: Waiting for a connection ${tail:text}
panels.description: Time a request queues for a connection before it reaches the database, at the chosen quantile. Should be near 0.

panels.title: Query latency ${tail:text}
panels.description: Database operations, every repository, at the chosen quantile (client side).

panels.title: Failed queries / s
panels.description: Database operations that did not succeed. Must be 0.

panels.title: DB pool in use
panels.description: Checked-out connections / pool size, per pool. Pinned at 100% means the pool is the bottleneck, not the database. Empty if `postgres.pool-metrics-interval` is not set for this service.

targets.expr: sum by (pool_name) (db_client_connection_count{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="$service", state="used"}) / clamp_min(sum by (pool_name) (db_client_connection_max{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="$service"}), 1)

panels.title: Waiting for a DB connection
panels.description: Time a request spends queued before it even reaches the database (seconds), and how many are queued. Should be ~0; anything visible is added straight to user latency.

panels.title: DB connection timeouts / s
panels.description: Requests that gave up waiting for a database connection (connection-timeout). Empty is healthy; any value is a request that failed because the pool was exhausted for the whole timeout. Empty if `postgres.pool-metrics-interval` is not set for this service.

panels.title: Query latency
panels.description: How long database operations take, every repository and method together: p50, p95, p99 and the selected Tail quantile. p99.99 needs roughly 10 000 requests in the rate window to mean anything and p99.999 roughly 100 000; both are rounded up to the histogram bucket edge. Client side: it includes the network and, for a pooler, the pooler's wait.

panels.title: Queries / s by operation
panels.description: The eight busiest database operations. Pair with the slowest-queries panel: a slow query that runs rarely matters less than a medium one that runs constantly.

panels.title: Slowest queries (${tail:text})
panels.description: The five slowest database operations by repository and method. First place to look when latency rises but the pool is fine.

targets.expr: topk(5, histogram_quantile($tail, sum by (le, repository, operation) (rate(db_client_operation_duration_seconds_bucket{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="$service"}[$__rate_interval]))))

panels.title: Failed queries / s
panels.description: Database operations that did not succeed. Empty is healthy.

panels.title: WAL headroom
panels.description: The WAL rate the checkpoint settings allow, divided by the rate now. Below 1× WAL is written faster than max_wal_size / checkpoint_timeout allows: checkpoints start from volume instead of the timer, which writes more full-page images, which is more WAL. 99× means idle. The 1× line is the documented boundary; Postgres can start a checkpoint a little before it, so treat 1–2× as close.

panels.title: Checkpoints on request
panels.description: Share of checkpoints in the selected time range that were started by WAL volume rather than the timer. The aim is 0%; anything else means max_wal_size is too small for the write rate.

targets.expr: max(increase(db_checkpoints_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="$service", type="requested"}[$__range])) / clamp_min(max(increase(db_checkpoints_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="$service", type="timed"}[$__range])) + max(increase(db_checkpoints_total{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="$service", type="requested"}[$__range])), 1)

panels.title: max_wal_size now
panels.description: The database's current setting.

panels.title: max_wal_size suggested
panels.description: 2 × the peak WAL rate of the last hour × checkpoint_timeout: the rule of thumb in loadgen-runbook/docs/07-wal-tuning.md. Compare with the setting on the left. It is a starting point; it needs disk for that much pg_wal.

panels.title: Idle replication slots
panels.description: Replication slots nothing is reading from. WAL is kept for them without limit, which is the usual way pg_wal fills a disk. Must be 0. Red as soon as there is one; which one and how much it holds is in the graph below.

targets.expr: sum(max by (slot) (db_replication_slot_active{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="$service"}) == bool 0) or (max(db_wal_retained_by_slots_bytes{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="$service"}) * 0)

panels.title: WAL held by slots
panels.description: The most WAL any one replication slot is holding back from being recycled.

panels.title: WAL written against what checkpoints allow
panels.description: WAL rate against the rate this database's own settings allow. Above the dashed line checkpoints come from volume, not the timer. Raise max_wal_size (see the suggested value above) or checkpoint_timeout.

panels.title: Checkpoints per minute
panels.description: timed = started by checkpoint_timeout, requested = started because WAL reached max_wal_size. Mostly timed is healthy; a rising 'requested' is the same problem as the headroom tile, seen from the other side.

panels.title: Full-page images in the WAL
panels.description: Approximate share of WAL that is whole 8 KiB pages (images x 8 KiB, before compression). A large share is what wal_compression and fewer checkpoints reduce; see loadgen-runbook/docs/07-wal-tuning.md.

panels.title: WAL records / s and bytes per record
panels.description: Record rate from pg_stat_wal and the average record size. Bytes per record rises with full-page images and falls with wal_compression; the rate follows the write load (logins, token rotations). The services publish no per-commit wait metric; the cost of a commit shows in the `Slowest queries` p99 of the database row below.

panels.title: WAL held back by replication slots
panels.description: Per slot. A line that only climbs for a slot with nothing reading it is the disk filling. Drop the slot if its consumer is gone. Empty when the database has no slots.

panels.title: $service — Data volume and cleanup of expired rows
Expired rows waiting
panels.description: Rows past their expiry that are still in the database, across every table with an expires_at. Counted up to a cap per table, so a very large backlog reads as at least that. Near 0 is healthy.

panels.title: Data in each table
panels.description: Every table with an expires_at, plus users. Rows is the database's estimate (refreshed by autovacuum). Size is exact and includes the table's indexes. Expired counts rows past their expiry that are still there, up to a cap; empty for a table with no index on expires_at.

panels.title: Expired rows waiting to be removed
panels.description: Is cleanup keeping up? Per table, the rows that should already be gone. A healthy table saws back to near 0 after each run; a line that only climbs is a table cleanup is losing to. Counted up to a cap per table.

panels.title: Live and expired rows
panels.description: How fast is the data growing? Rows still valid against rows past their expiry and not yet removed. Live is the size estimate minus expired, so it is approximate too.

targets.expr: clamp_min(max by (table) (db_table_rows_estimate{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="$service", table=~".*"}) - on (table) max by (table) (cleanup_expired_rows{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component="$service", table=~".*"}), 0)

panels.title: How overdue the oldest expired row is
panels.description: How long ago the oldest row that should already be gone expired. Unlike the count it has no cap. With cleanup keeping up it stays within about one cleanup interval of the table; a line that keeps climbing is a table whose cleanup has stopped.

panels.title: Rows removed / s
panels.description: How fast cleanup deletes expired rows, per table. Compare with the growth of the table: removal below the expiry rate is a backlog building.

panels.title: Time since the last successful cleanup
panels.description: Per table, how long ago a cleanup batch last succeeded. Resets at each run; a line that keeps climbing past a few cleanup intervals is cleanup stalled or failing (see the service's log).

panels.title: Tables without cleanup (count)
panels.description: Tables that have an expires_at column but no cleanup configured: what expires there is never removed. Must be 0. Red as soon as there is one; the list is on the right. A service that does not report it counts as one. No data means neither service is reporting it yet.

targets.expr: sum(max by (app_kubernetes_io_component, table) (cleanup_configured{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component=~"auth|edge"}) == bool 0) + (2 - count(count by (app_kubernetes_io_component) (cleanup_configured{namespace="$namespace", app_kubernetes_io_component=~"auth|edge"})))

panels.title: Which tables have no cleanup
panels.description: Which tables, in which service. Empty when every table with an expiry is cleaned. To fix one, add it to the service's cleanup tables in its config.
